newsitem.title: CANADA: Market divided on odds of Bank of Canada rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Market divided on odds of Bank of Canada rate cut.

text.p: A decision by the U.S. Federal Reserve on Tuesday to leave U.S. interest rates at current levels has renewed speculation that the Bank of Canada will soon lower short-term rates here, analysts said on Wednesday.
But market watchers remain divided over whether Canada's central bank will take the opportunity to cut interest rates for the eighth time this year.
"The market is very much split on what the Bank will or won't do following the Fed's inaction," said Anita Lauria, an economist with Salomon Brothers.
The Canadian money market has rallied sharply since the Fed decision, partly pricing in a Bank of Canada ease.

Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill last traded at 3.73 percent, compared with 3.88 percent just before the announcenment. The three-month cash bill traded at 3.87 percent, compared with 3.95 percent.

The Bank of Canada was seen being on hold ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee meeting on concern the Fed would hike rates 25 basis points. Now that the FOMC will not be meeting again until early November, many think Canada's central bank has a window of opportunity to cut rates further.

Those expecting the central bank to ease monetary policy said Canada's output gap of about 3.0 percent and inflation rate of just 1.4 percent provide the Bank of Canada with both the incentive and leeway to cut rates further.

"I think it's very likely. There's a lot of excess capacity in the Canadian economy," said Barry Davenport, senior vice-president of treasury with Bank of Montreal. "If they see there's a window open which will enable them to provide a rate cut I think they'll take that opportunity."
Another incentive for the central bank to lower rates is spending cuts by Canadian governments, analysts said.
These spending cuts, aimed at reducing government deficits, will result in "fiscal drag" on the economy over the next several years which can be partially offset by lower interest rates.
Market watchers sceptical that the central bank will cut rates counter that there are several major factors which more than offset the reasons for a rate cut.

The reason cited most often is the easing already done by the Bank of Canada. Since May, 1995 the central bank has cut rates by 400 basis points. This year alone it has cut seven times, six of those independent of any Fed easings.

"The bank doesn't necessarily have to ease anymore. Let's face it. They've done a lot of easing that's coming through the system," said Michael Gregory, an economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers.
Gregory and other analysts noted that recent economic indicators, including employment growth, suggest past easings by bank are already begun to stimulate the economy.

"We're seeing some evidence that the economy is getting back on its feet to some extent. That might suggest an on hold stance particularly in light of the significant easing that the Bank has done," said Salomon's Lauria.

Lauria said Salomon's position is that the Bank of Canada signalled after its most recent rate cut on August 22 that it has eased enough to boost growth. In the press release announcing the ease, the Bank said "the cumulative monetary ease now in place is substantial and can be expected to have a positive impact on the economy over the next year or so."

Investors are now focusing on the value of the Canadian dollar for signals as to whether the Bank of Canada will cut further, analysts said. If the dollar, which gained following the Fed decision, appreciated further it would tighten overall monetary conditions in Canada, making exports less attractive.
Analysts said this could prompt the Bank of Canada to cut rates in order to rebalance monetary conditions.

The Bank of Montreal's Davenport said the central bank could cut if the Canadian dollar continues to trade near current levels at C$1.3663 and an appreciation to C$1.3635 would definitely trigger a cut.
Gregory said the currency would have to appreciate much more sharply than that to trigger a cut.
He said unless the currency "catches fire" and trades to the C$1.35 level the Bank will not cut rates to offset currency appreciation.
